news.2026-10-23-afrique-du-sud-taxe-carb: South Africa trims its fuel tax on petrol and diesel, but lowers its growth forecast
The finance minister announces a temporary cut in the fuel levy, worth about 10 billion rand. In the same speech, the Treasury revises its 2026 growth forecast down.
On 21 October, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana presented his mid-year budget with a temporary fuel levy cut worth about 10 billion rand [1][3].
The levy falls by 1.50 rand per litre for petrol and 3 rand for diesel from 4 November to 1 December; smaller cuts then run until 5 January 2027 [3][4].
The Treasury lowers its 2026 growth forecast to 1.2%, from 1.6% in February, citing fuel prices, geopolitical tensions and the El Niño weather phenomenon [1][5].
The first thing to remember: a state chooses to give up public money so that filling the tank costs less, at the very moment it admits its economy is slowing [1][4].

The cost of the measure is offset by money that was going to the Central Energy Fund and now goes back to the state budget [2]. Public debt, for its part, stabilised at 78.4% of GDP in 2025/26 and is due to fall to 76.6% by 2030, according to the minister [3].
When oil gets more expensive, a country has to choose between helping drivers and keeping its accounts in order. It is the dilemma of any state facing costly oil.

news.2026-10-23-senegal-greve-generale-s: In Senegal, a three-day general strike reaches even the public electricity company
A front of unions stops work on 21, 22 and 23 October. At Senelec, they reject splitting the company into subsidiaries and demand that the state pay what it owes.
The Front syndical pour la défense du travail (FSDT) has called a 72-hour general strike on 21, 22 and 23 October, across the public, private and informal sectors [1].

At Senelec, the public electricity company, the SUTELEC union is joining the movement. It rejects splitting the company into subsidiaries, demands a bonus (the PRAB, close to 3 billion CFA francs according to the unions) and asks the state to settle a debt the unions put at more than 600 billion CFA francs [1][3].

Senelec's management says it received no formal notice and calls for dialogue [2]. In early October, the energy minister said the company would become a holding company (a parent company) by the end of 2027 [1].
The first thing to remember: when a country's electricity is at the heart of a standoff between unions and the state, the whole economy can slow down [1][2].
The figures on the state's debt to Senelec come from the unions and have not been confirmed by an official source. The real scale of the strike is not confirmed by an independent source [1].
An electricity company in financial difficulty means possible power cuts and delayed investment. It also affects French or European companies that produce or invest in Senegal.

news.2026-10-23-badr-pacte-defense-qatar: Qatar, Pakistan, Türkiye and Indonesia pool their arms factories
Four countries from very different regions sign the 'Badr' pact in Doha to produce and train together. It is not a military alliance: nobody promises to defend the others.
On 21 October in Doha, Qatar, Pakistan, Türkiye and Indonesia signed the 'Badr' memorandum of understanding on the defence industry [1][2].
It provides for joint military production, joint technical and military training and research, so that each country can use the defence capabilities of the other three [1].

Reports stress that this is industrial cooperation, not a mutual defence pact, and is separate from the other agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. The full text has not been published [1][4].
The first thing to remember: four countries want to produce weapons together rather than just buy them, sharing technology and supply chains [3][4].

Türkiye's defence procurement agency (SSB) explains that the pact turns existing two-country projects into a four-country framework. They include Turkish drones and armoured vehicles for Qatar, corvettes built for Pakistan's navy and a tank developed with Indonesia [3]. Qatar's minister also said Qatar would soon announce a local defence production hub [1].
When new countries make their own weapons, the world market changes: fewer orders for traditional sellers, more competition, and defence budgets turning to other suppliers.

news.2026-10-23-canada-turquie-partenari: Canada seeks gas, nuclear power and weapons deals in Türkiye to depend less on the United States
In Ankara, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan launch a 'strategic partnership' with a three-year action plan. Free-trade talks open next month.

On 22 October in Ankara, Mark Carney and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan launched the Canada-Türkiye strategic partnership, built on four pillars: trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and ties between peoples, with a three-year action plan [1][2].
They want to advance on liquefied natural gas, civil nuclear power, renewables and critical minerals. Carney said he wants to sell Türkiye Candu reactors, critical minerals and liquefied gas [1].
The two countries' export credit agencies, EDC and Türk Eximbank, are signing an agreement for joint projects in third countries, and free-trade negotiations will begin next month [1].
The first thing to remember: Canada is looking for other customers and partners to cut its dependence on the United States, and it is turning to Türkiye [4].
Before the visit, the press announced big contracts. The official texts mainly speak of commitments to cooperate, and no specific reactor contract appears in them [1][3].
When two NATO allies move closer on gas and nuclear power, it sketches new energy routes and new arms markets, which also affect prices in Europe.

news.2026-10-23-equateur-colombie-petrol: Ecuador lets Colombian oil flow through its pipelines again, after nine months of trade war
Petroecuador resumes transporting Colombian crude, halted since January. The two neighbours had clashed with tariffs.
Petroecuador has resumed transporting crude for Ecopetrol and Amerisur in its pipelines, after a suspension that began in January [1][3].
Deliveries had stopped on 23 January, after a decision that raised the transport fee for foreign oil on the SOTE pipeline from 3 to 30 dollars [1][5].
Ecuador carries an average of 11,900 barrels a day of Colombian crude, which should bring it about 1.4 million dollars a month, or 16.8 million dollars a year [1][2].
The first thing to remember: a pipeline can become a trade weapon, and its reopening marks the end of a fight between two Andean neighbours [1][3].

The conflict also hit tariffs: Ecuador announced 30% duties on Colombian goods, and Colombia hit back [4]. After months of tariffs and a ruling by the Andean Community, Quito and Bogotá are talking again [4].
Oil routes do not only run through big straits: a pipe between two small countries can also block exports. It is a reminder of why energy prices depend on politics.

news.2026-10-23-taiwan-micron-greve-puce: In Taiwan, workers at Micron, an AI-chip giant, go on strike to share in the profits
The union at the Taoyuan plant announced a work stoppage on Thursday 22 October. It wants a permanent profit-sharing scheme. The plant makes memory chips for artificial intelligence.
Micron's Taoyuan union had announced it would strike on Thursday 22 October, in support of the Taichung union, which is negotiating with management [1].
A newsletter citing Nikkei Asia says employees walked out of the plant at 9 a.m. for a 24-hour stoppage [3].

In the vote, 1,994 members, or 99% of those voting, approved the strike. Micron had offered a bonus of 1 million Taiwan dollars (about 31,400 US dollars) per employee, but the union wants a permanent profit-sharing mechanism [1].
The first thing to remember: a strike at a memory-chip plant, the chips at the heart of artificial-intelligence servers, can weigh on the whole global chain [1].

The Central Taiwan Science Park authority warned that the strike could affect the country's economy, and President Lai Ching-te urged both sides to negotiate 'sincerely' [1]. The length of the strike had not been announced as of 20 October [1].
Micron's memory chips (DRAM and HBM) end up in AI servers, computers and phones. A lasting blockage could make some components scarcer and more expensive.

news.2026-10-23-pakistan-afghanistan-com: Pakistan-Afghanistan: a year of closed border, and trade between the two countries collapses by 74%
Pakistan halted all trade with Afghanistan in October 2025. Trade fell from 1.3 billion to 358 million dollars, and Pakistani exporters are losing millions every month.
According to official Pakistani data published on 19 October, trade with Afghanistan fell by about 74% in 2025-26, from 1.3 billion to about 358 million dollars [1][3].
Pakistan has halted all commercial activity with Afghanistan since 10 October 2025; the Torkham crossing has been closed since deadly clashes [2][3].
Pakistani exporters are losing about 50 billion rupees (≈ 177 million dollars) a month, according to Arab News. A ceasefire was announced on 19 October, but trade remains suspended [2].
The first thing to remember: a closed border costs both sides dearly, and Pakistan risks permanently losing the Afghan and Central Asian markets [2].
Pakistani officials say trade routes will stay closed until security problems are resolved [2]. The ceasefire is reported by only one source, so it should be treated with caution [2].
When a major trade corridor closes, trade shifts to other routes that are longer and more expensive. It is one more example of how fragile Central Asian routes are.

news.2026-10-23-bulgarie-deficit-eurosta: Bulgaria: Eurostat raises the 2025 deficit to 4% and doubts the numbers of the euro's newest member
The EU statistics office has revised Bulgaria's 2025 deficit upward and raises questions about data quality. Bulgaria is already under a European excessive deficit procedure.
On 21 October, Eurostat raised Bulgaria's 2025 public deficit by 0.5 points, to 4% of GDP, and questioned the quality of the data sent by Sofia [1].
The European Union opened an excessive deficit procedure against Bulgaria seven months after it joined the euro area [2].
The EU Council had asked Bulgaria to present corrective measures by 15 October 2026 [3]. It is not yet known whether it did so.
The first thing to remember: a country that has just joined the euro is being criticised for both a deficit that is too large and numbers that are not reliable [1][2].
In the euro area, budget rules are shared: a deficit judged excessive can trigger a procedure and requests for corrections [2][3].
When a euro-area member slips, it concerns everyone who shares the currency: market confidence and budget rules are discussed together.

news.2026-10-23-kazakhstan-azerbaidjan-c: Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan agree on a simpler 'Middle Corridor' between China and Europe
The two countries sign an agreement so that trains and ships on the China-Europe route across the Caspian Sea coordinate better. Other countries will be able to join.
On 20 October, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan signed an agreement to simplify rail operations on the 'Middle Corridor', the freight route between China and Europe [1].
The two countries commit to a guaranteed minimum capacity, whose figure has not been published, and to give priority to each other's ships in their ports [1].
The agreement provides for a single transport document for the rail-and-ship journey, and other countries will be able to join [1].
The first thing to remember: one single document and guaranteed priorities are what make a transport route truly usable for companies [1].
The guaranteed amount is not public, so the effect on volumes cannot yet be measured [1].
The simpler and more predictable this route is, the more it can serve as an alternative to sea routes, which are currently disrupted by tensions around Hormuz.
